BREAKING: China’s central bank officially bought +20 tonnes of gold in August, matching its largest monthly purchase since October 2023.

This follows +20 tonnes and +15 tonnes acquired in July and June, respectively, and marks its 22nd consecutive monthly gold purchase.

So far in 2026, China has officially added +80 tonnes to its gold reserves, lifting total holdings to a record 2,387 tonnes.

By comparison, in full-year 2025, China increased its official gold reserves by a total of +29 tonnes.

In troy ounces, China added ~650,000 ounces to its reserves last month, taking its total holdings to a record 76.73 million ounces.

China continues to stockpile gold at a historic pace.

The AI Revolution is fueling a record financing boom in the US:

US high-grade corporate bond issuance is expected to surge to ~$215 billion in September, the largest September issuance on record.

This is set to surpass the previous September high of ~$205 billion, posted in 2025.

The current estimate is also more than triple the ~$70 billion issued in September 2022.

This follows $145.2 billion of US high-grade bonds issued in August, the highest August total on record, as AI-related data center buildouts continue to fuel corporate borrowing.

US companies have already borrowed more than $410 billion so far in 2026, specifically to fund data centers and other AI-related investments.

Meanwhile, retail investors have purchased more investment-grade bonds this year than in any full year in data going back to 2010.

The AI boom is driving a record corporate borrowing spree.

tweets.text:
From the Bitcoin pivot through June 2026, common shares increased by roughly 1.13bn. 60%+ of those came after June 2025 after the stock peaked. 

In fairness to management, as far as I can tell the Series 10 ratchet was disclosed in the March 2024 annual report just days before the Bitcoin pivot, and again in the March 2025 annual report. The April 2024 Bitcoin announcement did not highlight it, and the quarterly/half-year filings appear to have disclosed the outstanding rights but not the 20% ratchet mechanics. (Happy to be corrected here).

We should also concede the history: Simon was running a tiny distressed microcap when Series 10 was designed in...2022? A huge equity incentive in that situation is not that crazy.

So this was not hidden. An investor doing the work could have found it. The trickiness of dealing with Japanese disclosures, despite my fluency in Japanese, thankfully kept me from owning 3350 in any size after we exited that month.

Management also did a good job growing BTC per share. Had they simply tied comp to that, they still could have made $$$ for the accretion. They did their jobs.

Unfortunately, the windfall produced by the 20% ratchet has become grotesque relative to the company’s current market cap and the stock’s performance since the peak, and leaves management imperfectly aligned with shareholders from here.

Disclosure: I bought a little today. The stock is cheap, I'm more bullish on Bitcoin these days and more willing to take varying exposures. It's not so hard, though perhaps personally a bit expensive, to make things right going forward.

tweets.text:
After reading this, I can’t shake the feeling that we may already be living in a Three-Body world—one in which humanity is gradually, and perhaps inevitably, dividing itself into three camps: the Adventists, the Redemptionists, and the Survivors.

The Adventists want the Trisolarans to come. They see the arrival of a superior intelligence not as an existential threat, but as a potential replacement for a civilization they believe has reached its limits.

The Redemptionists also believe the Trisolarans can save us—but they hope that the two civilizations can coexist, with superior intelligence serving as a means of transcending the flaws of human civilization rather than replacing it.

The Survivors, by contrast, ask a much more primitive question: How do we survive the Trisolarans? For them, the preservation of human agency and human civilization takes precedence over the promise of whatever the future intelligence might bring.

What makes the analogy increasingly unsettling is the rapid emergence of superintelligence.

Perhaps we have already begun to fall, consciously or unconsciously, into these three camps. Some are eagerly anticipating the arrival of something greater than ourselves. Some believe AI will ultimately redeem humanity from many of the constraints that have defined our civilization. And some are increasingly preoccupied with a more fundamental question: whether humans will remain the ones making the decisions in the world we are creating.

The most interesting question, then, may not be whether superintelligence will transform human civilization. That increasingly seems inevitable.

The deeper question is which of these three visions of the future will ultimately prevail—and what happens when the people holding them begin competing for control over the intelligence that will shape that future?

Perhaps the future of AI will be determined not simply by how intelligent machines become, but by the relative dynamics and power of the Adventists, the Redemptionists, and the Survivors among us.
